question: The country of HMMTLand has $8$ cities. Its government decides to construct several two-way roads between pairs of distinct cities. After they finish construction, it turns out that each city can reach exactly $3$ other cities via a single road, and from any pair of distinct cities, either exactly $0$ or $2$ other cities can be reached from both cities by a single road. Compute the number of ways HMMTLand could have constructed the roads.

completions.text:
We will show that any road‐network satisfying the conditions must consist of two disjoint “cliques” (complete graphs) on 4 cities each. (In other words, the only 3–regular graph on 8 labeled vertices in which every pair of adjacent vertices has exactly 2 common neighbors and every pair of nonadjacent vertices has 0 common neighbors is the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.) Once that is proved, the answer is just the number of ways to split 8 labeled cities into two unlabeled groups of 4 (since on any set of 4 labeled vertices there is exactly one way to “fill in” all 6 possible roads to get K₄).

Let’s explain in detail.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Show that every vertex’s three neighbors form a triangle

Suppose the 8 cities are vertices and a road is an (undirected) edge. We are told that every city is connected by a single road to exactly 3 other cities (so every vertex has degree 3) and that for any two distinct cities the number of other cities that are connected by a single road to both is either 0 or 2.

Now, fix a vertex v and let its three neighbors be a, b, and c. Consider the pair a and b. They are both neighbors of v. There are two possibilities:
• If a and b were not connected by a road, then v and a would have only c as a common neighbor. But v and a are adjacent, and by hypothesis adjacent vertices must have exactly 2 common neighbors. This contradiction shows that a and b must be connected.
• The same argument shows that a and c, and b and c, must also be connected.

Thus the three neighbors of any vertex form a triangle.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Show that the whole graph is “forced” to be two disjoint K₄’s

Now, take any vertex v with neighbors a, b, and c (which, as we have seen, form a triangle). Look at the edge joining v and a. Since v and a are adjacent they must have exactly 2 common neighbors. But v’s neighbors are exactly a, b, and c so the only possibility is that a’s other two neighbors (besides v) are b and c. In other words, a is adjacent to v, b, and c. Repeating the same argument for b and c shows that
  v, a, b, and c
induce a complete graph K₄.

Now consider any city x that is not among {v, a, b, c}. City x also has degree 3. One might try to “attach” x to the K₄ by making it adjacent to one or more of v, a, b, or c. However, if x were adjacent to even one vertex in the K₄ then (by a short check using the “common neighbors” condition) one would be forced into a contradiction. (For example, if x were adjacent to v and also to, say, a, then v and x would have common neighbors v’s neighbors {a, b, c} intersected with x’s neighbors; one finds that for one of the vertices in {a, b, c} the count would be off.) A careful check shows that x cannot be adjacent to any vertex in the K₄. Thus x’s three neighbors must all lie outside {v, a, b, c}.

Repeating the argument shows that the remaining 4 vertices also “clump together” to form a K₄. In other words, the only possibility is that the 8 vertices split into two groups of 4 with every pair inside a group joined by a road and no road connecting the two groups.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Count the number of constructions

A construction is determined by choosing which 4 of the 8 cities form one of the K₄’s (the other 4 automatically form the other K₄). However, the two K₄’s are “unlabeled” (swapping the two groups does not change the road network). Therefore the number of ways is

  (Number of 4–element subsets of an 8–element set) ÷ 2 = C(8, 4) ÷ 2.

We compute C(8, 4) = 70, so the answer is 70 ÷ 2 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

There are 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed the roads.

We will show that the only way to “build the roads” (that is, to choose a set of two‐way roads between 8 distinct cities) so that

  (1) each city is connected by a road to exactly 3 other cities, and
  (2) for every pair of distinct cities the number of cities joined by a single road to both is either 0 or 2,

is (up to isomorphism) to take the 3–regular “cube–graph” on 8 vertices. (In other words, the only graph on 8 labeled vertices satisfying the stated conditions is the 3–dimensional cube, and once you “label” its vertices the number of different graphs you get is 8!/|Aut(Q₃)|.)

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A. The Graph Theoretic Reformulation

Label the 8 cities as vertices. A “road” is an edge, and “reaching by a single road” means that two cities are adjacent. Condition (1) says that every vertex has degree 3. (A graph in which every vertex has the same degree is called “regular” – here 3–regular.) Condition (2) says that for any two distinct vertices u and v the number
  c(u,v) = |N(u) ∩ N(v)|
(where N(u) is the set of neighbors of u) is either 0 or 2.

A few observations are in order:

1. Notice that if u and v are adjacent then they already “share” the edge uv. Thus if c(u,v) were positive it would have to be at least 1. In fact, one may show that if an edge uv were to have c(u,v) = 2 then writing
  N(u) = {v, a, b} and N(v) = {u, a, b},
one quickly runs into a contradiction when one looks at the edge joining u to a (its common neighbors would then be only {v} rather than 0 or 2). (A short “local‐analysis” shows that no edge may have 2 common neighbors.) Hence every edge (i.e. every pair of adjacent vertices) must have c(u,v) = 0.

2. Since every vertex has degree 3 the total number of 2–paths (that is, pairs of vertices connected by a vertex in common) is
  Σ (over vertices) C(3,2) = 8·3 = 24.
On the other hand, every pair of distinct vertices (and there are 28 such pairs) contributes either 0 or 2 to this total. Writing x for the number of pairs with 2 common neighbors we deduce
  2x = 24 ⟹ x = 12.
Thus exactly 12 pairs of vertices (whether adjacent or not) have exactly 2 common neighbors and the remaining 16 pairs have 0 common neighbors.

3. In any cubic graph on 8 vertices the possible distances between vertices are 1, 2, or 3. (One may show that if a cubic graph on 8 vertices were to contain a triangle then some adjacent pair would have exactly 1 common neighbor – forbidden by (2).) In fact, one may check that in the unique (up to isomorphism) bipartite cubic graph on 8 vertices the following happens:
  – If two vertices are adjacent then they have 0 common neighbors.
  – If two vertices are not adjacent and are at distance 2 then they have exactly 2 common neighbors.
  – If two vertices are not adjacent and are at distance 3 then they have 0 common neighbors.

It turns out that the only cubic graph on 8 vertices with these properties is the 3–dimensional cube (often denoted Q₃).

──────────────────────────────
B. The Cube Graph Q₃

One may describe Q₃ as follows. Think of the 8 vertices as the 3–bit binary strings:
  000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111.
Two vertices are adjacent if and only if their binary strings differ in exactly one coordinate. (It is easy to check that every vertex has degree 3.) One may then verify that:

• If two vertices are adjacent then they have no common neighbor (so c(u,v) = 0).
• If two vertices are not adjacent then either they are “two apart” (in which case they have exactly 2 common neighbors) or “three apart” (in which case they have 0 common neighbors).

Thus Q₃ satisfies condition (2).

──────────────────────────────
C. Counting the Labeled Constructions

Since the cities are labeled (say, 1,2,…,8) any construction is a labeled graph isomorphic to Q₃. (In other words, although Q₃ is unique up to isomorphism, many different labelings of its vertices yield non–isomorphic labeled graphs.) In general the number of labeled copies of a fixed graph G on n vertices is

  n! / |Aut(G)|,
 
where |Aut(G)| is the order of the automorphism group of G.

For the cube graph Q₃ the full automorphism group (which includes reflections) is isomorphic to the full symmetry group of the cube and has order 48. (The rotational symmetries alone would give 24, but here “graph automorphisms” count reflections as well.) Therefore the number of labeled copies is

  8! / 48 = 40320 / 48 = 840.

──────────────────────────────
D. Final Answer

There are exactly 840 ways for HMMTLand to construct the roads.

Thus, the answer is 840.

We will show that the only road‐network (i.e. graph) on 8 labeled cities satisfying

  (1) every city is connected by a single road to exactly 3 other cities (so the graph is 3–regular), and  
  (2) for every two distinct cities the number of cities joined by a single road to both is either 0 or 2

must be the disjoint union of two copies of the complete graph K₄. (In other words, the 8 vertices split into two groups of 4 and within each group every pair of vertices is joined by an edge.) Once this is proved the answer is “number of ways = (number of ways to choose 4 of the 8 cities to form one K₄) divided by 2 (since the two K₄’s are unordered) = C(8,4)/2 = 70/2 = 35.”

Let’s explain why no other graph can work.

Step 1. Reformulating the condition

Label the cities 1,…,8 and think of a “road” as an edge. Condition (1) says the graph G is 3–regular (each vertex has degree 3). Condition (2) says that for any two distinct vertices u and v the number
  |N(u) ∩ N(v)|              (where N(u) is the set of neighbors of u)
is either 0 or 2.

In particular, if u and v are adjacent then u ∈ N(v) and v ∈ N(u) so u and v already have one common neighbor (namely each other’s “role” in the edge) – but by (2) they must have exactly 2 common neighbors. Thus every edge uv has exactly two common neighbors.

Step 2. A consequence for neighborhoods

Now fix any vertex v and let its three neighbors be a, b, and c. Notice that v is a common neighbor of a and b (since both are adjacent to v). By the rule for edges, the edge ab must have exactly 2 common neighbors. One of these is v, so there is a unique other vertex, say x, such that x is adjacent to both a and b. But then a and b already have v and x as common neighbors. In other words, the three neighbors of v (namely a, b, and c) cannot be arbitrary; in fact, one may show that they must “pair up” so that for every edge among them the “other” common neighbor is forced. A short analysis shows that the only possibility is that the three neighbors of every vertex form a triangle. (For example, if v’s neighbors were a, b, c and if a and b were not adjacent then the edge ab would have only the common neighbor v, contradicting (2).)

Step 3. Deducing the structure

Now take any edge uv. We know u and v have exactly 2 common neighbors; call them w and x. But then, as just argued, the neighbors of u are exactly {v, w, x} and those of v are {u, w, x}. In other words, u, v, w, and x form a complete graph on 4 vertices (a K₄). But then u (and likewise v, w, and x) has no “room” to be adjacent to any vertex outside this K₄ because u already has degree 3. Thus the vertices u, v, w, and x “close up” as an isolated component. Since every vertex must have degree 3 and a 3–regular graph on fewer than 4 vertices is impossible, the entire graph must break up into components each of size 4. And on 4 vertices the only 3–regular graph is K₄.

Step 4. Counting the constructions

We have shown that any graph satisfying the conditions is exactly the disjoint union of two copies of K₄. (Note that the problem makes no assumption of connectivity so a disconnected graph is allowed.) To count the number of distinct road–networks on 8 labeled cities, we must choose which 4 cities form one K₄; the remaining 4 automatically form the other K₄. However, the two K₄’s are “unlabeled” (swapping the two groups does not produce a new network). Therefore the number is

  [Number of ways] = ½ · C(8,4) = ½ · 70 = 35.

Thus, the number of ways HMMTLand could have constructed the roads is 35.

We will show that any “road‐network” satisfying the conditions must be one of exactly two types. (In other words, if we view the 8 cities as vertices and a road between two cities as an (undirected) edge, then a “good” network is a simple graph on 8 labeled vertices in which

  (1) every vertex has degree 3, and 
  (2) for every two distinct vertices x and y the number
    f(x,y) = |{ z : z is adjacent to both x and y }|
is either 0 or 2.)

In what follows the phrase “by a single road” means “via an edge.”

Let us explain.

Step 1. What does the condition say about an edge?

Suppose x and y are adjacent. Then x’s three neighbors are
  N(x) = { y, a, b }
and y’s three neighbors are
  N(y) = { x, c, d }.
Now, when we “forget” x and y themselves the condition says that
  |N(x)∩N(y)| ∈ {0,2}.
But note that if x and y are adjacent then (by definition) each is a neighbor of the other; so when we “remove” x and y the common‐neighbors set is
  N(x)∩N(y) = { a, b } ∩ { c, d }.
Thus the condition forces
  { a, b } = { c, d}.
In other words, whenever x and y are joined by a road the two “other” neighbors of x must equal the two “other” neighbors of y.

Step 2. Two cases arise

There are now two possibilities for a given edge xy.

Case 1. f(x,y) = 0.
Then the two “other” neighbors of x and of y are disjoint. (In particular, if x is adjacent to a and y is adjacent to c then a ≠ c.) In this case no two adjacent vertices share any common neighbor. (In any graph a common neighbor of two adjacent vertices would create a triangle.) In other words, the graph is triangle–free. (One may check that in any triangle–free cubic graph on 8 vertices the following happens: if x and y are adjacent then f(x,y)=0, while if x and y are not adjacent then sometimes f(x,y)=2 and sometimes f(x,y)=0. For example, the familiar 3–cube (whose vertices may be identified with 3–bit strings) has the property that if two vertices are at distance 2 then they have exactly 2 common neighbors, while if they are at distance 3 the intersection is empty.)

Case 2. f(x,y) = 2.
Then, as we have seen, if x and y are adjacent and
  N(x) = { y, a, b } and N(y) = { x, a, b },
then look at the edge x–a. Applying the same reasoning to x–a we deduce that
  N(x)∖{a} = N(a)∖{x}.
But N(x)∖{a} = { y, b } so that N(a) = { x, y, b }.
A similar argument shows that N(y) = { x, a, b } and N(b) = { x, y, a }.
Thus the four vertices x, y, a, b form a complete graph K₄ (every two are adjacent) – and in a K₄ every edge “sees” the other two vertices as common neighbors.

Now observe that if even one edge of the network has f = 2 then the endpoints of that edge (together with their “shared” two neighbors) form a K₄. But then every vertex in that K₄ has degree 3 and no vertex outside can be adjacent to any vertex in the K₄ (for if, say, some vertex w were adjacent to a vertex in the K₄ then by applying the rule to the edge joining w to that vertex one would “force” w also to be adjacent to the other two vertices in the K₄ – which would “use up” all three of w’s roads). In other words, the whole network would break up as the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.

Step 3. The only two possibilities

Thus any network satisfying (1) and (2) is either

  (a) a connected graph on 8 vertices in which every edge has f = 0 – and one may show that (up to isomorphism) the only such cubic graph is the 3–cube (sometimes called the “cube graph”), or

  (b) a disconnected graph consisting of two disjoint copies of K₄.

A quick check shows that in a K₄ every pair of vertices is adjacent and, when the two vertices are removed, the remaining two vertices are common to both – so f = 2 for every edge in a K₄. Also, if two vertices lie in different K₄’s then they are not adjacent and have no common neighbor – so f = 0.

Step 4. Counting the labeled networks

Since the cities are labeled (say, 1,2,…,8) we must count the number of labeled graphs isomorphic to one of the two types.

Type (a): The cube graph.
It is well known that the symmetry group of the cube has 48 elements. (One may show that Aut(cube) ≅ S₄.) Hence the number of labeled copies of the cube graph is
  8!⁄48 = 40320⁄48 = 840.

Type (b): Two disjoint copies of K₄.
To form such a graph we must partition the 8 vertices into two unlabeled sets of 4. (Once a set of 4 is chosen, the graph induced on it is uniquely K₄.) The number of ways to choose a 4–element subset from 8 is C(8,4) = 70, but since the two components are “unlabeled” we must divide by 2!; that is, there are 70⁄2 = 35 such graphs.

Step 5. The final answer

Adding the two cases we obtain
  840 + 35 = 875.
Thus there are 875 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed its roads.

Answer: 875.

We will show that under the stated conditions the only possibility is that the 8 “cities” (vertices) break up into two disjoint sets of 4 so that on each set every city is joined by a road to every other city in that set (that is, each set forms a complete graph K₄). (In other words, the only 3‐regular graph on 8 vertices in which every two distinct vertices have either 0 or 2 common neighbors is the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.) Once this is proved the answer is “35” because there are 
  ½·C(8,4) = 35 
ways to split 8 labeled vertices into two unlabeled groups of 4.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion.

───────────────────────────── 
A “common‐neighbors” count

Suppose the cities are represented by the vertices of a graph G on 8 vertices. We are told that

(1) Each city reaches exactly 3 others by a single road. In graph–theory language G is 3–regular (every vertex has degree 3).

(2) For any two distinct cities (vertices) the number of “other” cities that can be reached from both by a single road is either 0 or 2. In other words, for any two distinct vertices x and y the number
  |N(x) ∩ N(y)|
(where N(v) is the set of neighbors of v) is either 0 or 2.

Now, count in two ways the number of “2–paths” (that is, ordered pairs of distinct vertices joined by a middle vertex). On one hand, every vertex v (having degree 3) lies in C(3,2) = 3 pairs of its neighbors so that the total (over all 8 vertices) is 8·3 = 24. On the other hand, every edge xy is “witnessed” by each common neighbor z of x and y. (Note that when we say “common neighbor” we mean a vertex different from both x and y.) Thus if we sum |N(x)∩N(y)| over all edges xy we also get 24.

But there are 12 edges in a 3–regular graph on 8 vertices (since 8·3/2 = 12) and each term in the sum is either 0 or 2. In order for the total to be 24 every edge must contribute exactly 2. (For if even one edge contributed 0 the total would be at most 11·2 + 0 = 22.) In other words, for every edge xy we must have

  |N(x) ∩ N(y)| = 2.

───────────────────────────── 
What does this force?

Now fix any vertex v and let its three neighbors be a, b, and c. Look at the edge va. Since v and a are adjacent we know
  |N(v) ∩ N(a)| = 2.
But v’s neighbors are exactly a, b, and c so that
  N(v) ∩ N(a) ⊆ {b, c}.
Since the intersection has size 2 it follows that both b and c lie in N(a) – that is, a is adjacent to both b and c. (A similar argument applied to the edges vb and vc shows that b and c are also adjacent to each other.) Thus the three neighbors of v form a triangle.

Now, look at a itself. We have seen that a is adjacent to v, b, and c. But a has degree 3 so its neighbors are exactly {v, b, c}. In other words, the four vertices v, a, b, and c form a complete graph K₄ (since every two of them are adjacent). But then every edge of G lies in a K₄ (namely, the unique K₄ determined by the three neighbors of one of its endpoints). In a 3–regular graph a vertex’s three neighbors “use up” all its edges, so no vertex can belong to two different K₄’s. Consequently the vertex set of G breaks up as the disjoint union of the vertex–sets of various K₄’s. Since a K₄ has 4 vertices and G has 8 vertices the only possibility is that G is the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.

One may check that in a K₄ every two distinct vertices are adjacent and have exactly the other two vertices as common neighbors, while vertices in different K₄’s are not adjacent and have no common neighbors. Thus the condition “either exactly 0 or 2 common neighbors” is met.

───────────────────────────── 
Counting the possibilities

The cities are labeled (that is, the 8 vertices are distinct). To “construct the roads” according to the rules is to choose a graph G on 8 labeled vertices that is isomorphic to two disjoint copies of K₄. But any such graph is determined by choosing a 4–element subset A of the 8 cities to form one K₄ (with all 6 edges present) and putting all the remaining roads in the complementary set V∖A. (The other copy is then forced.) However, the two K₄’s are “unlabeled” (that is, the order in which we choose them does not matter). Hence the number of such graphs is

  ½ · C(8,4) = ½ · 70 = 35.

───────────────────────────── 
Conclusion

The only way to satisfy the conditions is to have the road network consist of two disjoint copies of K₄, and there are exactly 35 ways to choose which cities form the two groups. Therefore, the answer is 35.

Answer: 35.

We will show that if a graph on 8 labeled vertices has the property that

  (1) every vertex is incident with exactly 3 edges (so the graph is “cubic”), and
  (2) for every pair of distinct vertices the number of common neighbors is either 0 or 2,

then the graph must be exactly two disjoint copies of the complete graph K₄.

In what follows the “cities” are the vertices and the “roads” are the (undirected) edges.

Step 1. Every vertex’s three neighbors must form a triangle.

Pick any vertex v and let its three neighbors be a, b, and c. Now consider the pair (a, b). There are two cases:
 • If a and b are not adjacent, then they are a non‐edge. By condition (2) nonadjacent vertices must have 0 common neighbors. But both a and b are adjacent to v, so they would have at least one common neighbor (namely, v) – a contradiction.
 • Hence a and b must be adjacent. The same argument shows that a and c, and also b and c, must be adjacent.

Thus the three neighbors of any vertex form a triangle.

Step 2. Every vertex “forces” a K₄.

Now look at vertex v with neighbors a, b, c. We have just shown that a, b, and c are mutually adjacent. But then consider vertex a. Its three neighbors are v, b, and c. (It cannot have any other neighbor, for then its degree would exceed 3.) In other words, the set {v, a, b, c} forms a complete graph K₄. (Indeed, every vertex in a K₄ is adjacent to the other three.) The same reasoning applies to b and c. Thus the vertex v “forces” that v together with its three neighbors form a K₄.

Step 3. The whole graph is a disjoint union of K₄’s.

Now suppose the graph has 8 vertices and is cubic. Pick any vertex v and form the K₄ on {v, a, b, c} as above. Since every vertex in this K₄ already has degree 3 (all within the K₄) no vertex in this K₄ can be adjacent to any vertex outside it (or else its degree would be more than 3). Therefore the remaining 4 vertices must form another K₄. In other words, the only possibility is that the graph is exactly the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.

Step 4. Verification of the conditions.

In a copy of K₄ every vertex has degree 3. Moreover, if two vertices lie in the same K₄ then they are adjacent and, being in a 4‐vertex complete graph, they have exactly the other 2 vertices as common neighbors. If two vertices lie in different K₄’s then they are not adjacent and have no common neighbors. Thus condition (2) is met.

Step 5. Counting the number of constructions.

The cities are labeled 1,…,8. A construction is determined by choosing a set of 12 edges (since a cubic graph on 8 vertices has 8·3⁄2 = 12 edges) that forms two disjoint copies of K₄. To count these we must partition the 8 labeled vertices into two unlabeled sets of 4 (each set will be the vertex set of a K₄) and then take all edges inside each 4‐set.

The number of ways to choose a 4–element subset from 8 is C(8,4) = 70. However, the two K₄’s are “unlabeled” (swapping the two parts does not produce a new construction), so we must divide by 2. Thus the total number is

  (1/2)·70 = 35.

Therefore, there are 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed the roads.

We will show that any road‐network satisfying

  (1) every city is joined by a road to exactly 3 others, and 
  (2) for every pair of distinct cities the number of “common‐neighbors” (that is, the number of cities joined by a single road to both) is either 0 or 2

must be (up to isomorphism) one of only two types of graphs on 8 vertices:
  • either the “cube‐graph” Q₃ (the 1–skeleton of a cube), or 
  • the disjoint union of two copies of K₄ (the complete graph on 4 vertices).

In what follows we explain one way to arrive at this conclusion and then count the number of labeled graphs (that is, assignments of the 8 distinct city–labels to the 8 vertices) of each type.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the conditions

Think of the cities as vertices and the roads as (undirected) edges. Condition (1) says that every vertex has degree 3 (a “cubic” graph on 8 vertices). Since a cubic graph on 8 vertices has (8·3)/2 = 12 edges, our graph G has 12 edges.

Condition (2) says that for every pair of distinct vertices u and v the number
  c(u,v) = |{ w ≠ u,v : w is adjacent both to u and to v }|
is either 0 or 2.

A useful observation is obtained by “double–counting” the number X of ordered triples (u,v,w) with u ≠ v and with w adjacent to both u and v. On one hand, since every vertex has 3 neighbors there are exactly 3 choices for a second neighbor at each vertex so
  X = 8·C(3,2) = 8·3 = 24.
On the other hand, if t is the number of unordered pairs {u,v} for which c(u,v)=2 then
  X = 2t   (since each such pair contributes 2).
Thus t = 12. In other words, among the 28 pairs of distinct vertices (since C(8,2)=28) exactly 12 pairs have two common neighbors and the remaining 16 pairs have none.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Which graphs can occur?

A short analysis shows that in any cubic graph satisfying (2) the following must hold:
  (a) No two neighbors of a given vertex can be adjacent (for if u and v were both neighbors of some w and also adjacent, then u and v would share w and one more common neighbor, contradicting “0 or 2”). In other words, every vertex’s neighborhood is an independent set.
  (b) In particular, G contains no triangles.
  (c) One may check that if G is connected then one may prove that every pair of non–adjacent vertices must be “close” (in fact, one may show that the only possibility is that G is isomorphic to the cube–graph Q₃). (For example, in Q₃ the vertices at distance 2 always have exactly 2 common neighbors while vertices at distance 3 have none.)
  (d) On the other hand, if G is disconnected then the only possibility is that G is the disjoint union of two cubic graphs on 4 vertices. But the only cubic graph on 4 vertices is K₄. (In K₄ every vertex is adjacent to the other 3, and any two vertices in the same K₄ have exactly the other 2 as common neighbors while vertices in different components have no common neighbor.)

One may check by a short case–analysis that among the (finitely many) cubic graphs on 8 vertices the only connected example having (2) is Q₃ and the only disconnected example is K₄ ∪ K₄.

Let us verify the two cases:

• Q₃ (the cube–graph):  
Represent the vertices by 3–bit binary strings. Two vertices are adjacent if they differ in exactly one coordinate. Then one may check that:
  – Any two adjacent vertices have no common neighbor.
  – Any two vertices at distance 2 (i.e. differing in exactly two coordinates) have exactly 2 common neighbors.
  – Any two vertices at distance 3 (opposites) have no common neighbor.
Thus condition (2) is met.

• K₄ ∪ K₄:  
In each copy of K₄ every vertex is joined to the other 3. Thus if two vertices lie in the same K₄ then they are adjacent and their common neighbors are exactly the other 2 vertices in that K₄. If the two vertices lie in different K₄’s then they are not adjacent and have no common neighbor. Again condition (2) holds.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Counting the labeled graphs

Since the cities are labeled (distinct), we must count the number of distinct graphs on the vertex set {1,2,…,8} that are isomorphic to one of the two types.

Case 1. Graphs isomorphic to Q₃

A standard fact is that the number of labeled copies of a given (unlabeled) graph H on n vertices is
  n! / |Aut(H)|.
For the cube–graph Q₃ it is known that |Aut(Q₃)| = 48 (this is the full symmetry group of the cube). Hence the number is
  8! / 48 = 40320 / 48 = 840.

Case 2. Graphs isomorphic to K₄ ∪ K₄

Here the graph is disconnected with the vertex set partitioned into two sets of 4. (There is no “wiggle–room” in labeling a complete graph on 4 vertices; once the 4 vertices are chosen the graph is forced.) Thus the number is found by first choosing which 4 of the 8 vertices form the first K₄ and then (automatically) the remaining 4 form the other K₄. There is no extra factor for automorphisms because on 4 vertices K₄ has automorphism group S₄ (of order 24) but the graph on 4 labeled vertices is unique. Therefore the number is
  C(8,4) = 70.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Adding the cases

The total number of ways to construct the roads is the sum from the two cases:
  840 + 70 = 910.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

There are 910 ways for HMMTLand to construct the roads.

Thus, the final answer is 910.

We will show that any graph on 8 labeled cities satisfying

  (1) each city is joined by a road to exactly 3 other cities (i.e. the graph is 3‐regular), and
  (2) for every pair of distinct cities the number of common neighbors is either 0 or 2

must in fact be exactly two disjoint copies of the complete graph K₄. (In K₄ every vertex is joined to the other 3, and any two vertices in K₄ have exactly the other 2 as common neighbors; if two cities lie in different copies there are no common neighbors.) Once this is proved the answer is immediate: the number of ways to “construct the roads” is the number of ways to partition the 8 labeled cities into 2 unlabeled groups of 4 (each group then gets all 6 roads of a K₄), and that number is

  ½·C(8,4) = ½·70 = 35.

Below is one way to justify the claim.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Show that if two cities are joined by a road then they “force” a K₄.

Suppose cities v and a are adjacent. Since v has degree 3 its neighbors are, say, a, b, and c. Now consider the pair (v, a). By condition (2) they have exactly 2 common neighbors. But v’s neighbors (besides a) are {b, c} so we must have
  N(v) \ {a} = N(a) \ {v} = {b, c}.
In other words, a’s other two neighbors are exactly b and c. Hence, a is joined to b and c as well. Similarly, looking at the edges (v, b) and (v, c) one deduces that b and c are adjacent. Thus the four cities v, a, b, and c form a K₄ (every pair among them is connected).

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Show that no city can “mix” between different K₄’s.

Now take any city v. Its three neighbors (say, a, b, and c) form a K₄ with v. Now suppose there were some other city w not in {v, a, b, c} that were adjacent to, say, a. Then by the same reasoning applied to the edge (a, w) we would have
  N(a) \ {v} = N(w) \ {a}.
But we already know N(a) \ {v} = {b, c} (since a lies in the K₄ with v, b, c). Thus w would also have to be adjacent to both b and c. In other words, w would belong to the K₄ on {v, a, b, c} – a contradiction. Therefore every city’s neighbors force it to lie in a unique K₄, and no road can connect vertices in different K₄’s.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Conclude the structure and count the possibilities.

Since every city lies in a K₄ and no road connects different K₄’s, the 8 cities must be partitioned into two disjoint groups of 4. In each group every city is connected to the other 3 (forming a K₄), and any two cities in different groups are not connected (so they have 0 common neighbors). This is exactly the graph described by the problem.

To count the number of such graphs on 8 labeled cities, note that the only choice is how to partition the 8 cities into 2 unlabeled groups of 4. There are C(8,4) = 70 ways to choose a 4‐element subset for the first group, but the two groups are unlabeled (swapping them does not produce a new construction), so we must divide by 2. This gives

  (1/2) × 70 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

There are 35 ways HMMTLand could have constructed the roads.

We will show that any road‐network (i.e. graph) on 8 labeled cities satisfying

  (1) every city is connected by a single road to exactly 3 other cities (so the graph is 3–regular), and 
  (2) for every two distinct cities the number of “common neighbors” (cities joined by a single road to both) is either 0 or 2,

must in fact be exactly the disjoint union of two copies of the complete graph K₄. (In other words, the 8 vertices split into two groups of 4, with every two vertices in the same group joined by a road and no road joining vertices in different groups.) Once this is proved the answer is “the number of ways to partition 8 labeled cities into two unlabeled sets of 4”, which is

  (1/2)·C(8,4) = (1/2)·70 = 35.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Show that every vertex’s neighbors form a triangle

Let the graph be G with vertex set V (|V| = 8) and suppose every vertex has degree 3. Now pick any vertex v and let its three neighbors be u, w, and x. (That is, N(v) = {u, w, x}.) Notice that u and w are both neighbors of v so they have at least the common neighbor v. But by hypothesis the number of common neighbors of any two distinct vertices is either 0 or 2. Since v is one common neighbor, u and w must have exactly one more common neighbor. In other words, u and w are adjacent. (A similar argument shows that every two distinct neighbors of v are adjacent.) Thus the three neighbors of v form a triangle.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Show that every edge “forces” a K₄

Now take any edge uv. Since u is adjacent to v, the triangle on the neighbors of u is N(u) = {v, a, b} for some vertices a and b. Similarly, v’s neighbors form the triangle N(v) = {u, c, d}. But u and v are both neighbors of each other so when you look at the pair (u,v) the hypothesis says they must have exactly 2 common neighbors (apart from each other). In other words, the sets {a, b} and {c, d} must have exactly 2 elements in common. (They cannot be disjoint since then u and v would have only the one common neighbor v or u respectively.) In fact, one may check that this forces
  N(u) = {v, a, b} and N(v) = {u, a, b}.
That is, u and v share the same “other” two neighbors. In any graph the “neighborhood” of a vertex is a clique (here, a triangle) and we see that the edge uv “comes with” a triangle on {u, v, a, b} which is nothing other than a copy of K₄.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Conclude that G is the disjoint union of two K₄’s

Start with any edge uv. By the argument in Step 2 the vertices u, v, a, b form a K₄. Now, look at any vertex (say, a) in this K₄. Its three neighbors are u, v, and b. But a 3–regular graph on 8 vertices has 12 edges in all, and one may show by a short “local‐analysis” that no vertex outside this K₄ can be adjacent to any vertex in it (for if, say, some vertex w outside were adjacent to u then u’s neighborhood would have to be {v, a, b, w}, contradicting the fact that it has exactly 3 neighbors). Thus the remaining 4 vertices (call them c, d, e, f) must form another component. Applying the same reasoning to that component shows it too is a K₄. (One may also check that if G were connected and had more than 4 vertices then starting with any edge one would “force” a K₄ and then no extra vertex could be added without destroying the property that every vertex’s neighbors form a triangle.)

Thus the only possibility is that G is exactly the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Count the number of such graphs

Since the cities are labeled the only “choice” is how to split the 8 cities into two groups of 4 (each group giving one copy of K₄). (Once the groups are chosen the roads are completely determined: every two cities in the same group are connected, and no road joins cities in different groups.) The number of ways to choose a 4–element subset from 8 is C(8,4) = 70. However, the two groups are “unlabeled” (the order in which we pick them does not matter), so we must divide by 2. Hence the total number is

  (1/2)·70 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

There are 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed the roads.

Thus, the answer is 35.

We will show that if 8 labeled cities are joined by roads so that

  (1) every city is joined by a road to exactly 3 others (i.e. the graph is 3‐regular), and
  (2) for every pair of distinct cities the number of cities joined by a road to both is either 0 or 2,

then the only possibility is that the 8 vertices split into two disjoint sets of 4 with every pair within a set joined by a road (that is, the graph is the disjoint union of two copies of K₄). (In any graph on labeled vertices “K₄” means the complete graph on 4 vertices.) Once this is shown the answer is immediate: the number of ways to choose an unordered partition of 8 labeled vertices into two sets of 4 is

  [ C(8,4) ]⁄2 = 70⁄2 = 35.

In what follows we explain one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Show that if two cities are connected by a road then they must have exactly 2 common neighbors.

Suppose cities u and v are joined by a road. Since u is joined to exactly 3 cities and one of these is v, the other 2 neighbors of u must be among the common neighbors of u and v. (The condition says that for any two distinct cities the number of common neighbors is either 0 or 2.) Thus if u and v are adjacent the number of common neighbors is 2. In other words, for every edge uv we must have

  N(u)∖{v} = N(v)∖{u},

where N(x) denotes the set of neighbors of x.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Deduce that the neighborhood of every city forms a triangle.

Fix a city u and let its three neighbors be v, w, and x. Look at the edge uv. By the conclusion of Step 1 we have
  N(u)∖{v} = {w, x} = N(v)∖{u}.
Similarly, considering the edge uw gives
  N(u)∖{w} = {v, x} = N(w)∖{u}.
Thus v and w (which are both neighbors of u) must be adjacent (since they appear together as the “other” neighbors for u when paired with v or w). A similar argument shows that every two of u’s three neighbors are adjacent. That is, the three neighbors of every city form a triangle.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Show that the only possibility is two disjoint copies of K₄.

Now, start with any city u. Its three neighbors form a triangle; call this set T = {v, w, x}. Because u is adjacent only to the three vertices in T, no other city is adjacent to u. Next, look at any vertex y not in T ∪ {u}. Since u and y are not adjacent, condition (2) forces
  N(u) ∩ N(y) = ∅.
But u’s neighbors are exactly T, so y cannot be adjacent to any vertex in T. Since y must have degree 3 it must be adjacent to all of the other cities outside T ∪ {y}. There are 8 − |T ∪ {u} ∪ {y}| = 8 − 5 = 3 such cities, and so the 4 vertices outside T ∪ {u} (which includes y and the 3 others) form a complete graph K₄. In other words, the vertex set splits into two parts: one part is {u, v, w, x} (which, by the discussion in Step 2, is K₄) and the other part is the remaining 4 vertices (which must form a K₄ as well because every vertex there has degree 3 and no vertex from the first part is adjacent to any vertex in the second part—if there were such an edge, then the two endpoints would share a neighbor, contradicting condition (2) for a non‐adjacent pair).

Thus the only graph on 8 vertices satisfying the conditions is the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Count the number of such graphs.

Since the cities are labeled the only “choice” is how to partition the 8 cities into two unlabeled sets of 4 (each set giving a copy of K₄). The number of ways to choose a 4‐element subset from 8 is C(8,4) = 70, but the two sets are unordered (the two K₄’s play the same role), so we must divide by 2. This gives

  70⁄2 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

There are exactly 35 ways for HMMTLand to construct the roads so that every city is joined to exactly 3 others and every pair of distinct cities has either 0 or 2 common neighbors.

The final answer is 35.

We will show that the only way to choose roads (i.e. edges) among 8 distinct cities (vertices) so that

  (1) every city is joined by a road to exactly 3 other cities (so the graph is 3‐regular), and
  (2) for every pair of distinct cities the number of “common neighbors” (cities joined by a road to both) is either 0 or 2,

is to have the road network be exactly the disjoint union of two copies of the complete graph K₄.

In what follows the “cities” are labeled (so different labelings count as different constructions).

Let’s explain.

Step 1. Reformulating the conditions

Suppose our graph G has 8 vertices and is 3–regular. Then the total number of edges is
  (8·3)/2 = 12.

The extra condition says that for any two distinct vertices u and v the number
  |N(u) ∩ N(v)|                  (“common neighbors”)
is either 0 or 2.

Now, if u and v are adjacent then u has 3 neighbors and one of these is v so that
  |N(u) ∩ N(v)| = |N(u) \ {v}| = 2.
But note that N(u) \ {v} is a 2–element set. (Likewise for v.) Thus if u and v are adjacent the only possibility is that
  N(u) \ {v} = N(v) \ {u}.
In other words, if two cities are directly connected by a road then, aside from each other, they share exactly the same two neighbors.

On the other hand, if u and v are not adjacent then the condition requires
  |N(u) ∩ N(v)| = 0,
so no city is connected by a road to both u and v.

Step 2. Deducing the structure

Now start with an arbitrary edge joining cities u and v. Write
  X = N(u) \ {v}   (so X is a 2–element set).
Then by the property we must have
  N(v) \ {u} = X.
Thus u’s neighbors are exactly {v} ∪ X and v’s neighbors are exactly {u} ∪ X.

Now look at any city w in X. Since w is adjacent to u (by definition of X) the edge (u, w) is present. For that edge the “other” two common neighbors of u and w must be exactly
  N(u) \ {w} = {v} ∪ (X \ {w}).
Thus w must be adjacent to v and to the unique other city in X. In other words, the four cities u, v, and the two members of X form a complete graph on 4 vertices (a K₄) because:
  • u is adjacent to v and the two in X,
  • v is adjacent to u and the two in X, and
  • each city in X is adjacent to u, v, and to each other.
In a K₄ every vertex has degree 3 and any two distinct vertices are adjacent (so they have the other 2 as common neighbors).

But then note: u and v already “used up” their 3 available neighbors. Hence no city outside this K₄ can be adjacent to u or v. (For if, say, u were adjacent also to some city outside, then for the edge (u, that city) the common neighbors would have to be a 2–element subset of N(u) = {v} ∪ X, but that would force that city to be adjacent to both v and the other member of X – and a short check shows that would contradict the 3–regularity.) In other words, every city “belongs” to one of these K₄’s.

Since there are 8 cities in all and every vertex has degree 3, the only possibility is that the 8 vertices break up into two disjoint sets of 4, with each set inducing a complete graph K₄. (Within a K₄ any two vertices are adjacent and share the other 2 as common neighbors; between vertices in different K₄’s there is no edge and hence no common neighbor.)

Step 3. Counting the number of constructions

The only road network that works is therefore the disjoint union of two copies of K₄. (It is not connected, but the problem makes no connectivity requirement.)

Now, the cities are labeled. To “construct the roads” we must choose which 4 of the 8 cities form one K₄ and the remaining 4 automatically form the other K₄. However, the two K₄’s are “unlabeled” (swapping them does not produce a different road network).

Thus the number of ways is the number of ways to partition an 8–element set into two unlabeled subsets of 4:
  Number = (number of 4–element subsets of an 8–set) / 2
      = C(8, 4) / 2 = 70/2 = 35.

Therefore, there are 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed the roads.

Final Answer: 35.

We will show that any graph on 8 labeled vertices satisfying

  (1) every vertex is incident with exactly 3 edges (“each city reaches exactly 3 others”), and 
  (2) for any two distinct vertices the number of common neighbors is either 0 or 2

must in fact be the disjoint union of two copies of the complete graph K₄. (In K₄ every vertex has degree 3, and if two vertices are adjacent then their “other” two neighbors are the same; if they are in different components then they have no common neighbor.) Once this is proved the answer is immediate: to get such a graph on 8 labeled vertices one must choose 4 of the 8 vertices to form one K₄ and the remaining 4 automatically form the other K₄. (Since the two components are “unlabeled” the number is ½·C(8,4) = 35.)

Below is one way to justify the claim.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the condition

Label the 8 cities (vertices) arbitrarily. The condition “each city can reach exactly 3 other cities” means the graph is 3–regular (cubic). Next, the statement “from any pair of distinct cities, either exactly 0 or 2 other cities can be reached from both cities” means that for any two distinct vertices u and v the number
  |N(u) ∩ N(v)| 
(where N(u) is the set of neighbors of u) is either 0 or 2.

Now, note that if u and v are adjacent then u ∈ N(v) and v ∈ N(u) but these “self‐references” are not counted when we say “other cities”. Thus for an edge uv we must have
  |N(u) ∩ N(v)| = 2.
Write
  N(u) = {v, a, b}  and  N(v) = {u, c, d}.
Since u ∈ N(v) and v ∈ N(u) the “other” neighbors (that is, N(u)∖{v} and N(v)∖{u}) must be equal (as 2–element sets) in order that their intersection have size 2. In other words, for every edge uv we have

  N(u)∖{v} = N(v)∖{u}.              (∗)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Deducing a “K₄–in a Nutshell”

Now fix any vertex u and let its three neighbors be v, w, and x. Apply (∗) to the edge uv:
  N(u)∖{v} = {w, x} = N(v)∖{u},
so that
  N(v) = {u, w, x}.
Similarly, applying (∗) to the edge uw gives
  N(w) = {u, v, x},
and to the edge ux gives
  N(x) = {u, v, w}.
Thus the four vertices u, v, w, and x have the property that every one of them is adjacent to each of the other three. In other words, they form a copy of K₄.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. The only possibility on 8 vertices

Since u was arbitrary, every vertex “sees” that its three neighbors form a triangle and that together with u they make a K₄. In particular, if the graph were connected then starting at any vertex we would be forced to remain in that K₄. But a K₄ has only 4 vertices, contradicting that there are 8. Hence the graph cannot be connected. In fact, the only possibility is that the vertex–set splits into two disjoint sets of 4 vertices, with each 4–set inducing a K₄. (One may check that in each K₄ the condition is satisfied: any two adjacent vertices have the other two as common neighbors, and any two vertices in different K₄’s have no common neighbor.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Counting the number of graphs

Now the cities are labeled. To form a graph of the required type we must partition the 8 labeled vertices into two unlabeled groups of 4. (On any given 4–set the only graph possible is K₄.) The number of ways to choose 4 vertices out of 8 is C(8,4) = 70, but since the two K₄’s are unordered we must divide by 2. Thus the total number is

  70/2 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

There are exactly 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed the roads so that each city reaches exactly 3 others and every pair of cities has either 0 or 2 common neighbors.

The final answer is 35.

We will show that the only way to “build the roads” (that is, to choose a set E of roads among the 8 labeled cities so that the resulting simple graph G has the property that

  (1) every vertex has degree 3, and
  (2) for every two distinct vertices u and v the number of common neighbors (i.e. the number of cities joined by a single road to both u and v) is either 0 or 2

) is to have G be the disjoint union of two copies of the complete graph K₄. (In K₄ every vertex is joined to the other 3, and any two distinct vertices have exactly the other 2 as common neighbors.) Once this is proved the answer is “the number of ways to partition 8 labeled vertices into two unlabeled sets of 4”, which is

  (1/2)·C(8,4) = (1/2)·70 = 35.

In what follows we explain one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Every city has degree 3

Since “each city can reach exactly 3 other cities via a single road” the graph G on 8 vertices has 8·3/2 = 12 edges and is 3–regular.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A key observation about neighborhoods

Pick any vertex v and let its three neighbors be a, b, and c. Now consider the edge joining v and a. Since v is adjacent to b and c, one of the common neighbors of v and a is already v’s “other” neighbors. But the condition requires that for every pair of distinct vertices the number of common neighbors is either 0 or 2. (It cannot be 1.) Thus, for the edge va the “missing” common neighbor must come from among a, b, and c. In other words, a must be adjacent to both b and c. (A similar argument applies to the edges vb and vc.) Hence the three neighbors of any vertex form a triangle.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. What happens for an edge?

Now suppose u and v are adjacent. Write
  N(u) = {v, x, y} and N(v) = {u, z, w}.
Look at the edge uv. Its common neighbors (besides u and v) come from N(u)∖{v} and N(v)∖{u}. In order for the number of common neighbors to be 2 (it can’t be 0 because v is already a common neighbor of u and one of its other neighbors), we must have
  {x, y} = {z, w}.
That is, whenever u and v are adjacent the “other two” neighbors of u and of v are identical. (For example, if u is adjacent to v, x, and y then v must be adjacent to u, x, and y.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Every vertex “lives” in a K₄

Fix a vertex v with neighbors a, b, and c. We have just seen that for the edge va the common neighbors are exactly {b, c} and similarly for the edges vb and vc. In particular, a, b, and c are all mutually adjacent. Thus the four vertices {v, a, b, c} form a complete graph K₄. (Note that in K₄ every vertex has degree 3 and every pair of distinct vertices has exactly the other 2 as common neighbors.)

Now suppose there were some vertex w not in {v, a, b, c} that were adjacent to one of v’s neighbors (say a). Then look at the edge wa. Since w is adjacent to a but not to v (because w ∉ {v, a, b, c}), one may check that w would have to be adjacent to both b and c (to make the common‐neighbor count for wa equal 2). But then w would belong to {v, a, b, c} – a contradiction. In other words, no vertex outside the K₄ containing v can be adjacent to any vertex of that K₄.

Thus every vertex v “forces” that its closed neighborhood N(v) ∪ {v} is a K₄. In particular, if u and v are adjacent then they lie in the same K₄. And if they are not adjacent then neither is adjacent to any vertex in the other’s K₄. (For if, say, u were adjacent to some vertex in N(v), then by the argument above u would have to be adjacent to all of N(v) and hence lie in the same K₄ as v.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. The graph is a disjoint union of two K₄’s

Since every vertex v has its closed neighborhood equal to a K₄ and no vertex outside that K₄ is adjacent to any vertex in it, the vertex set of G breaks up into disjoint “blocks” of 4. (One may show that a connected graph with the stated property cannot exist.) With 8 vertices the only possibility is that G is the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.

It is easy to check that a disjoint union of two copies of K₄ does indeed satisfy the conditions:
 • Each vertex has degree 3.
 • Any two vertices in the same K₄ are adjacent and have exactly the other 2 vertices (of that K₄) as common neighbors.
 • Any two vertices in different K₄’s are not adjacent and have no common neighbors.

──────────────────────────────
Step 6. Counting the number of constructions

The cities are labeled (say 1, 2, …, 8). A construction of the roads is given by choosing a partition of the 8 vertices into two unlabeled sets of 4 and then “putting in” all the roads within each 4–set (that is, taking the complete graph on each 4–set).

The number of ways to choose a 4–element subset from 8 is C(8,4) = 70. However, the two components are “unlabeled” (swapping the two groups does not produce a different road–network). Hence the number of distinct constructions is

  (1/2)·70 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

There are 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed the roads.

Thus, the answer is 35.

We are given 8 cities and a collection of two‐way roads (edges) between distinct cities (vertices) so that:

 • Each city is connected by a road to exactly 3 other cities (i.e. every vertex has degree 3).

 • For any two distinct cities, if you look at the set of cities that are directly connected to both, that set has either 0 or exactly 2 cities.

In graph–theoretic language, we are looking for a graph G on 8 vertices with

 (1) Every vertex has degree 3, and
 (2) For every pair of distinct vertices x and y, the number of common neighbors |N(x) ∩ N(y)| is either 0 or 2.

Step 1. Recognize the Strongly Regular Graph

A graph with these properties is a strongly regular graph. (A strongly regular graph with parameters (v, k, λ, μ) is one in which every vertex has degree k, every two adjacent vertices have exactly λ common neighbors, and every two non‐adjacent vertices have exactly μ common neighbors.) Here the condition “either 0 or 2” must hold for every pair of distinct vertices. In a strongly regular graph the numbers λ and μ are constant (though not every pair of vertices in a general graph must have the same number of common neighbors). Thus we have two possibilities:

 Case A. λ = 2 and μ = 0.
 Case B. λ = 0 and μ = 2.

Let’s check the feasibility of each.

For Case A, every adjacent pair has 2 common neighbors and every non–adjacent pair has 0. (We will soon see that this case indeed occurs.) For Case B, every adjacent pair would have 0 common neighbors and every non–adjacent pair 2. However, one may show by using standard formulas for strongly regular graphs that no graph with parameters (8, 3, 0, 2) exists. (For example, one of the eigenvalue formulas leads to non–integer multiplicities.) Thus the only possibility is Case A: λ = 2 and μ = 0.

Step 2. Identify the Graph

A well–known graph with parameters (8, 3, 2, 0) is the 3–dimensional cube (or “cube graph”). To check:
 • The cube has 8 vertices.
 • Each vertex (city) is incident with 3 edges (roads).
 • If two vertices are adjacent (i.e. connected by a road), they lie on a common face of the cube and share exactly 2 neighbors.
 • If two vertices are not adjacent, they do not share any common neighbor.

Thus the cube graph satisfies the conditions.

Step 3. Count the Number of Ways

Although the cube graph (as an abstract graph) is unique up to isomorphism, the cities are labeled (distinct). Therefore, two constructions that are isomorphic as graphs but with different assignments of the 8 cities to the 8 vertices are considered different.

The number of labeled graphs on 8 vertices that are isomorphic to a fixed graph G is given by

  (Number of labelings) = 8! / |Aut(G)|,

where |Aut(G)| is the order of the automorphism group of G.

For the cube graph (which is the 1–skeleton of the cube), its automorphism group is exactly the full symmetry group of the cube. (Any symmetry of the cube sends vertices to vertices and preserves adjacency.) It is known that the full symmetry group of the cube has 48 elements. (In fact, the automorphism group of the 3–cube Q₃ is isomorphic to (Z/2Z)³ ⋊ S₃, which has order 8·6 = 48.)

Thus the number of distinct constructions (labeled graphs) is

  8! / 48 = 40320 / 48 = 840.

Answer: There are 840 ways HMMTLand could have constructed the roads.

We will show that any graph on 8 labeled vertices satisfying

  (1) every vertex is incident with exactly 3 edges (i.e. the graph is 3‐regular), and
  (2) for every pair of distinct vertices the number of common neighbors is either 0 or 2

must in fact be the disjoint union of two copies of the complete graph K₄. (In K₄ every vertex has degree 3 and any two vertices – being adjacent – have the other 2 vertices as common neighbors.)

Below is one way to see this.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Show that every vertex’s neighbors must form a triangle

Pick any vertex v. By (1) v has 3 neighbors. Now, take any two distinct neighbors a and b of v. Since a and b are both neighbors of v, they have at least one common neighbor (namely, v). But condition (2) says that the number of common neighbors of any two distinct vertices is either 0 or 2. (It cannot be 1.) Therefore a and b must be adjacent. Since a and b were an arbitrary pair among the 3 neighbors of v, it follows that v’s 3 neighbors form a triangle.
──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Look at an edge and “grow” a K₄

Now take any edge uv. By (1) u and v each have 3 neighbors. Write
  N(u) = {v, a, b} and N(v) = {u, a, c},
where a is a common neighbor of u and v (forced by (2) since u and v are adjacent they must share exactly 2 common neighbors; we may call one of these a and the other, say, d—but as we shall see the structure forces a “K₄” to appear).

Since u’s neighbors {v, a, b} form a triangle, we have a, b, v all mutually adjacent. Similarly, since v’s neighbors {u, a, c} form a triangle, a, c, u are mutually adjacent. In particular, u, v, a, and (at least one of) b or c are all pairwise adjacent. A short check shows that in fact u, v, a, b, c must “collapse” into a K₄. (One may show by a similar argument that no vertex outside this K₄ can be adjacent to any vertex of it – otherwise that vertex’s degree would exceed 3.)

Thus the vertices that lie in the neighborhood “clusters” of u and v form a K₄.
──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Conclude the graph splits as two disjoint K₄’s

Now, every vertex v has its 3 neighbors forming a triangle. In the argument above we saw that if two vertices are adjacent then “around” that edge one finds a K₄. But note that in a K₄ every vertex already has degree 3. Hence no vertex in a K₄ can be adjacent to any vertex outside that K₄ (or its degree would be more than 3). In other words, the graph “breaks up” into components in which every vertex has degree 3 and, as we have just seen, the only 3‐regular graph on 4 vertices is K₄.

Since there are 8 vertices in all and 3‐regular graphs on 4 vertices exist only when the number of vertices is 4, the only possibility is that the graph is the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.
──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Count the number of labeled graphs of this type

The cities (vertices) are labeled. To form a graph of the required type we must partition the 8 labeled vertices into 2 unlabeled sets of 4. (Once a set of 4 is chosen, the unique 3‐regular graph on 4 vertices is K₄.) The number of ways to choose a 4‐element subset from 8 is

  C(8,4) = 70.

However, the two components are “unlabeled” (the order in which we choose them does not matter), so we must divide by 2. This gives

  70/2 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

There are exactly 35 ways for HMMTLand to construct the roads so that every city is connected by a single road to exactly 3 other cities and every pair of distinct cities has either 0 or 2 common neighbors.

The final answer is 35.

  (1/2)·C(8,4) = (1/2)·70 = 35.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Every vertex’s three neighbors form a triangle

Suppose the 8 cities are the vertices of a graph G and an edge means “there is a road between the two cities.” Condition (1) says every vertex has degree 3. Now fix any vertex v and let its three neighbors be a, b, and c. Look at the pair a and b. Since both a and b are adjacent to v, the condition (2) applied to the pair (a,b) tells us that
  |N(a) ∩ N(b)| ∈ {0, 2}.
But v is a common neighbor of a and b. (Remember that no vertex is considered a neighbor of itself.) Hence |N(a) ∩ N(b)| is at least 1. It cannot be 1 (since the only allowed numbers are 0 or 2) so it must be 2. In other words, a and b have exactly two common neighbors and one of them is v; therefore there is a unique other vertex (call it, say, x) with x adjacent to both a and b. In particular a and b must be adjacent. The same argument shows that a and c are adjacent and that b and c are adjacent. Thus the three neighbors of v form a triangle.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Every edge “forces” a K₄

Now take any edge uv. We already know that v’s three neighbors (one of which is u) form a triangle. In particular, if we write
  N(v) = {u, a, b},
then a and b are adjacent. Now look at the edge ua. Applying the same reasoning to the pair (u,a) we see that u and a must have exactly two common neighbors. But u is adjacent to v, a, and b (its three neighbors) and a is adjacent to u, v, and (by the triangle on v) b. Thus the only way for u and a to have two common neighbors is that
  N(u) = {v, a, b}  and  N(a) = {u, v, b}.
In other words, the edge uv “forces” the situation that u and a share the same two other neighbors. In summary, if u and v are adjacent then
  N(u) = {v, a, b}  and  N(v) = {u, a, b}.
That is, u, v, a, and b form a complete graph K₄.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. The whole graph is the disjoint union of two K₄’s

Now, every vertex v has degree 3 and its three neighbors form a triangle. From Step 2 we see that for any edge uv the “extra” two common neighbors force u and v to lie in a K₄. One may now show that no vertex can belong to two different K₄’s. (For if v lay in two different K₄’s then v would have at least 3+3–1 = 5 neighbors, contradicting that its degree is 3.) Hence the 8 vertices break up into two disjoint sets of 4, with the graph on each set being the complete graph K₄. (Notice that within each K₄ every pair of vertices is adjacent so the “common‐neighbors” condition is satisfied by having exactly the other 2 as common neighbors, while vertices in different K₄’s are not adjacent and have no common neighbors.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Counting the labeled graphs

Since the cities are labeled (that is, the 8 vertices are distinct) the only “choice” is how to partition the 8 cities into two unlabeled groups of 4. (Once the groups are chosen the roads in each group are forced to be all the possible roads—that is, each group yields a copy of K₄.)

The number of ways to choose a 4–element subset from 8 is C(8,4) = 70. However, the two groups are “unlabeled” (the order in which we pick them does not matter), so we must divide by 2. This gives

  (1/2)·70 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

There are exactly 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed its roads under the given conditions.

Thus, the answer is 35.

We will show that under the stated conditions the only possibility is that the 8‐vertex graph is exactly the disjoint union of two copies of the complete graph K₄. (In other words, the 8 cities are partitioned into two groups of 4, and every city in a group is joined by a road to every other city in that group; no road connects a city in one group with a city in the other.) Once this is proved the answer is immediate: a partition of 8 labeled cities into two unlabeled sets of 4 can be done in

  (1/2)·C(8,4) = (1/2)·70 = 35

different ways.

In what follows we explain one way to arrive at this conclusion.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Translate the conditions into graph–theory language

Label the 8 cities as vertices. A “road” is an edge, and since roads are two–way the graph is undirected. The condition “each city can reach exactly 3 other cities via a single road” means that every vertex has degree 3 (the graph is “cubic”). Also, “from any pair of distinct cities, either exactly 0 or 2 other cities can be reached from both cities by a single road” means that for any two distinct vertices u and v the number of common neighbors |N(u) ∩ N(v)| is either 0 or 2.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Show that if two vertices are adjacent then they “share” the same two other neighbors

Suppose u and v are adjacent. Since u has degree 3 its neighbors are {v, x, y} (for some vertices x and y). Similarly, v’s neighbors are {u, x′, y′}. But the condition applied to the pair u,v tells us that
  |N(u) ∩ N(v)| = 2.
Since u and v are adjacent, neither is in its own neighborhood so we must have
  {x, y} = {x′, y′}.
In other words, if u and v are joined by an edge then aside from each other they have exactly the same two neighbors.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Conclude that every vertex “sees” a triangle among its neighbors

Fix a vertex v. It has 3 neighbors; call them a, b, and c. Now, look at the edge va. By the conclusion of Step 2 the two neighbors of v other than a (namely b and c) must equal the two neighbors of a other than v. In particular, b and c are adjacent. The same reasoning applies to the edges vb and vc. Thus the three neighbors of v form a triangle (that is, a, b, and c are pairwise adjacent).

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Show that a connected graph with more than 4 vertices cannot work

Now suppose for contradiction that the graph were connected and had more than 4 vertices. Pick any edge uv. Then by Step 2 the two neighbors of u besides v (call them a and b) equal the two neighbors of v besides u. Thus the four vertices u, v, a, and b form a K₄ (the complete graph on 4 vertices). Now, look at one of the neighbors of, say, a. Since a has degree 3 its neighbors are {u, v, c} for some vertex c not among {u, v, a, b}. But then consider the edge ac. Applying the rule to a and c we see that the two neighbors of a other than c (namely u and v, together with b) must equal the two neighbors of c other than a. In order for c to have only 3 neighbors this forces c to be adjacent to all four vertices u, v, a, and b – an impossibility since that would give c degree 4. (A similar contradiction is reached by any other choice.) Hence no connected cubic graph on 8 vertices can satisfy the condition.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Conclude that the only possibility is two disjoint copies of K₄

Since the graph is cubic on 8 vertices it has 12 edges. The only 3–regular graph on 4 vertices is K₄ (which has 6 edges). Therefore the only way to “split” 8 vertices into components that are each 3–regular is to have two disjoint copies of K₄. (Note that if two vertices lie in different components then they are not adjacent and clearly have no common neighbors, which is allowed by the condition.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 6. Count the number of labeled graphs of this type

A graph of the required type is determined by choosing which 4 of the 8 labeled cities form one of the K₄’s (the other 4 then form the other K₄). However, the two components are “unlabeled” (that is, it does not matter which one we call “first” or “second”). Thus the number of ways is

  (1/2)·C(8,4) = (1/2)·70 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

There are 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed the roads.

Thus, the answer is 35.

We will show that the only graph (on 8 labeled cities) satisfying

  (1) each city is joined by a road to exactly 3 other cities, and
  (2) for every pair of distinct cities the number of “other” cities joined by a road to both is either 0 or 2

is exactly the disjoint union of two copies of the complete graph K₄. (In K₄ every vertex is joined to the other 3, and any two distinct vertices are either adjacent – in which case they share the other 2 vertices – or non‐adjacent – and then share no vertex.) Once this is proved the answer is obtained by “counting” the ways to partition 8 labeled cities into two unlabeled groups of 4 (each group giving a K₄).

Let’s explain in detail.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Reformulating the conditions

View the cities as vertices and the roads as (undirected) edges. Then condition (1) says the graph is 3–regular on 8 vertices. Condition (2) says that for any two distinct vertices u and v the number of common neighbors (that is, the number of vertices joined by an edge to both u and v) is either 0 or 2.

In particular, if u and v are adjacent then they must have exactly 2 common neighbors; if they are not adjacent then they have 0 common neighbors.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Analyzing an edge

Pick any edge joining two cities u and v. Since u and v are adjacent, they must have exactly 2 common neighbors. Denote these by a and b. Thus
  N(u) = {v, a, b}  and  N(v) = {u, a, b}.
(Here N(x) denotes the set of neighbors of x.)

Now look at the edge joining u and a. Since u and a are adjacent their common neighbors (other than each other) must be exactly 2. But u’s neighbors other than a are {v, b} so a must be adjacent to both v and b. That is,
  N(a) = {u, v, b}.

A similar argument shows that
  N(b) = {u, v, a}.

Thus the four vertices u, v, a, and b form a complete graph K₄ (each vertex is adjacent to the other three).

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. What about the remaining vertices?

So far we have found a K₄ on 4 of the 8 vertices. Now take any vertex w not among {u, v, a, b}. We claim that w cannot be adjacent to any vertex in this K₄. (For suppose w were adjacent to, say, u. Then u and w are adjacent so they must have exactly 2 common neighbors. But u’s neighbors are {v, a, b} so w would have to be adjacent to two of these. Then one may check that for one of those vertices (say v) the condition would force w to be adjacent to all three of u, v, and one of {a, b} – impossible since w’s degree is 3.) 

Thus every neighbor of w lies outside the K₄. But there are 8 – 4 = 4 vertices outside the K₄, and w (being 3–regular) must be adjacent to 3 of them. In other words, the subgraph induced on the 4 vertices outside the K₄ is complete (each vertex in that set is adjacent to all the other 3). That is, the 4 vertices outside form a K₄.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Conclusion

We have shown that any graph satisfying the conditions must consist of two disjoint copies of K₄. (One may also check that in such a graph any two vertices in the same K₄ are adjacent and share the other 2 vertices, while any two vertices in different K₄’s are not adjacent and share no vertex – exactly as required.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Counting the constructions

Since the cities are labeled the “construction” is determined by specifying which 4 cities form one K₄ (with all 6 roads among them) and the remaining 4 form the other K₄. However, the two K₄’s are “unlabeled” (swapping the two groups does not produce a different set of roads).

The number of ways to choose a 4–element subset from 8 is C(8,4) = 70. Since the two groups are unordered we must divide by 2. Hence the number of distinct graphs is

  70/2 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

There are 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed the roads.

We will show that under the stated conditions the only possible road‐network (i.e. graph) on 8 labeled cities is the disjoint union of two copies of K₄ (the complete graph on 4 vertices). (In other words, the 8 cities split into two groups of 4, and every city is joined by a road to each of the other 3 cities in its group; there are no roads between the two groups.) Once this is proved the answer is obtained by “choosing” which 4 cities form one group (the other 4 automatically form the other group), and then noting that in each group the road‐network is forced (namely, all 6 possible roads among 4 cities are built). (Since the two groups are “unlabeled”, one must divide by 2.) We now explain.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Translating the conditions

Label the cities 1,…,8 and imagine that a “road” is represented by an (undirected) edge. The conditions say that

(1) Every city is joined by a road to exactly 3 other cities. (That is, the graph is 3–regular.)

(2) For any two distinct cities (vertices) u and v the number of other cities joined by a road to both u and v is either 0 or 2. In graph–theory language, for any two distinct vertices u and v the number |N(u) ∩ N(v)| is either 0 or 2.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Deducing that every vertex’s neighbors form a triangle

Fix a vertex v and let its three neighbors be, say, a, b, and c. Now, consider the pair a and b. They are both neighbors of v so v lies in N(a) ∩ N(b). By condition (2) we must have
  |N(a) ∩ N(b)| = 2.
But v is one common neighbor of a and b, so there must be exactly one other city (say, w) that is adjacent both to a and to b. In other words, a and b share exactly the two neighbors v and w. In particular, a and b are adjacent. (A similar argument shows that a and c, and b and c, are adjacent.) Thus the three neighbors of v form a triangle.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. “Swapping” neighborhoods along an edge

Now take any edge joining two cities u and v. Since u’s neighbors form a triangle and v is one of them, write
  N(u) = {v, x, y}.
Similarly, since v’s neighbors form a triangle and u is one of them, we may write
  N(v) = {u, x, y}.
Thus u and v “share” the same two other neighbors. In other words, whenever two cities are directly connected the “pattern” of their three roads is forced.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Showing the graph “breaks up” into two K₄’s

Now start at any vertex v. We have seen that its three neighbors (call them a, b, and c) are all mutually adjacent. Therefore the four vertices {v, a, b, c} form a K₄. (In a K₄ every vertex is adjacent to the other three.) One may then show that if any other city were joined by a road to one of these four then a “mismatch” would occur in the common–neighbor counts. (A short “chasing the neighborhoods” argument shows that no vertex outside {v, a, b, c} can be adjacent to any vertex in that set without forcing, for some adjacent pair, an intersection of neighborhoods of size other than 2.) In other words, every city’s three roads must lie entirely within a set of 4 cities that forms a K₄.

But a 3–regular graph on 8 vertices cannot be connected unless it is a K₄ (which has only 4 vertices). (In any connected cubic graph on more than 4 vertices the “swapping” property forces overlaps that eventually lead to a contradiction.) Hence the only possibility is that the 8 vertices break up into two disjoint 4–vertex sets and on each set every pair of cities is connected by a road. In other words, the network is exactly the disjoint union of two copies of K₄.

──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Counting the number of networks

The cities are labeled. To “build” a network we must partition the 8 labeled cities into two (unlabeled) groups of 4. (On each group the roads are forced: every pair of cities in that group is joined by a road.) The number of ways to choose a 4–element subset from 8 is

  C(8,4) = 70.

However, since the two groups are unordered (choosing group A then group B is the same as choosing group B then group A), we must divide by 2. Thus the total number is

  70/2 = 35.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

There are exactly 35 ways for HMMTLand to construct the roads so that every city is joined to exactly 3 others and every pair of cities has either 0 or 2 common neighbors.

The answer is 35.

(In other words, the only 3–regular graph on 8 vertices in which every two distinct vertices have either 0 or 2 common neighbors is Q₃.) Then, since the cities are labeled, the number of different “road–systems” is just the number of labelings of Q₃. (Any two labeled graphs that are isomorphic give a different “construction”.)

Step 2. The extra condition is that for every pair of distinct vertices u and v the number
  c(u,v) = |{w : w adjacent to both u and v}

We are given 8 distinct cities (vertices) and a set of two‐way roads (edges) with the following properties:

1. Each city is connected by a road to exactly 3 other cities. In graph–theory language, the graph is 3–regular (cubic) on 8 vertices.
2. For any two distinct cities, if you look at the set of cities that are directly connected to both, then that set has either exactly 0 or exactly 2 elements.

We will show that these conditions force the graph to be exactly two disjoint copies of the complete graph K₄.

Step 1. What happens when two cities are connected by a road?

Suppose cities u and v are adjacent. Since the graph is 3–regular, u is connected to v and two other cities; call them x and y. Similarly, v is connected to u and (two other) cities. For the condition to hold for the pair (u, v) we must have that u and v share exactly 2 common neighbors. In other words, the two “other” neighbors of u must equal the two “other” neighbors of v. That is, 
  N(u) = {v, x, y} and N(v) = {u, x, y}.
Thus, u, v, x, and y are all mutually connected. (Note that even though the condition does not force x and y to be adjacent a priori, if they were not, then looking at the pair (x, y) we would have N(x) = {u, v, ?} and N(y) = {u, v, ?} and by the “adjacent–vertices” argument applied to (x, y) they would have to share the same “third” neighbor – forcing an edge between x and y. In any event, one may check that the only possibility is that u, v, x, and y form a complete graph on 4 vertices, K₄.)

Step 2. What happens when two cities are not connected by a road?

Now suppose u and v are not adjacent. The condition tells us that the number of common neighbors of u and v is either 0 or 2. (One may try to “force” the 2 case, but it leads to a contradiction as shown below.) Assume for contradiction that u and v have 2 common neighbors, say x and y. Then u is connected to v, x, y and v is connected to u, x, y. But then consider the pair (u, x). Since u and x are adjacent, they must share exactly 2 common neighbors. u’s neighbors are {v, x, y} and x’s neighbors (apart from u) would have to include the same two vertices. A similar argument applied to (u, y) forces that x and y are common neighbors of u. But then look at the pair (x, y): They are both adjacent to u and v so they would have at least these 2 common neighbors. In fact, one can check that if one tries to “mix” vertices from different groups, one eventually runs into a situation where some pair of adjacent vertices would end up with only 1 common neighbor. (A careful check shows that the only way to satisfy the condition for every pair is to have no “cross–talk” between different groups.) 

Thus, if u and v are not adjacent, they must have 0 common neighbors.

Step 3. The only possibility

We have now deduced:
• If two cities are adjacent, then they lie together in a set of 4 cities which form a K₄.
• If two cities are not adjacent, then they have no common neighbors.

This exactly describes the disjoint union of two copies of K₄. In a K₄ every vertex has degree 3 and any two vertices (which are adjacent) share the other two vertices as common neighbors. Moreover, any two vertices in different K₄’s are not adjacent and have no common neighbors.

Step 4. Counting the number of such graphs

Since the cities are labeled (distinct), a construction is determined by choosing which 4 cities form one K₄ and the remaining 4 automatically form the other K₄. (Note that the K₄ on any set of 4 vertices is unique, since it is the complete graph on 4 vertices.) However, the two K₄’s are “unlabeled” (the order in which we choose them does not matter), so we must divide by 2 to correct for over–counting.

The number of ways to choose 4 cities out of 8 is 
  C(8, 4) = 70.
Dividing by 2 (since the two groups are unordered) gives 
  70/2 = 35.

Thus, there are 35 ways for HMMTLand to have constructed the roads.

Final Answer: 35.
